title: Adjective gender agreement
explanation: Italian adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in gender. Masculine nouns take masculine adjective endings, feminine nouns take feminine endings. For 4-form adjectives: masculine ends in -o (rosso), feminine ends in -a (rossa). For 2-form adjectives: the form is the same for both genders (triste).

title: 2-form adjectives — gender doesn't change the ending
explanation: Some Italian adjectives have the same form for masculine and feminine. Only number changes: singular ends in -e, plural ends in -i. Do not add -a for feminine — the singular form is the same for both genders.

examples.en: the heavy bag (feminine singular — same form)
the heavy bags (feminine plural — same form)

examples.it: il mare tranquillo / la città tranquilla

title: Adjective number agreement
explanation: Italian adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in number. Singular nouns take singular adjective endings, plural nouns take plural endings. For 4-form adjectives: masculine plural ends in -i (rossi), feminine plural ends in -e (rosse). For 2-form adjectives: plural ends in -i regardless of gender (tristi).

title: Invariable adjectives
explanation: Some Italian adjectives do not change form for gender or number. Common examples are colour words borrowed from other languages or nouns used as colours: blu (blue), rosa (pink), viola (purple). Use the same form regardless of the noun.

title: Definite articles
explanation: The definite article ('the') in Italian depends on the gender of the noun and the first letter(s) of the following word. Masculine singular: il (standard), lo (before z, s+consonant, ps, gn, x, y), l' (before vowels). Masculine plural: i (standard), gli (before z, s+consonant, vowels). Feminine singular: la (standard), l' (before vowels). Feminine plural: le.

title: Indefinite articles
explanation: The indefinite article ('a' / 'an') in Italian: un (masculine standard), uno (masculine before z, s+consonant, ps, gn, x, y), una (feminine standard), un' (feminine before vowels). There is no plural indefinite article; use the partitive (dei, delle) or no article.

title: Noun gender
explanation: Every Italian noun has a grammatical gender — masculine or feminine. Gender is not always predictable from the ending. Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine (gatto, libro) and those ending in -a are usually feminine (casa, ragazza), but there are important exceptions. 'Mano' (hand) ends in -o but is feminine. 'Problema' (problem) ends in -a but is masculine (like many words of Greek origin). Gender must be learned with each noun.

title: Noun plurals
explanation: Most Italian nouns form their plural by changing the final vowel: -o → -i (gatto/gatti), -a → -e (ragazza/ragazze), -e → -i (cane/cani). Some nouns have irregular plurals that must be memorised: uomo/uomini, mano/mani. Nouns ending in an accented vowel do not change in the plural: città/città.

title: Ci sono / C'è
explanation: 'C'è' means 'there is' (singular). 'Ci sono' means 'there are' (plural). These are fixed constructions used to state that something exists or is present. Unlike English, the word order does not change for questions — intonation signals the question.

title: Possessives require the definite article
explanation: Italian possessives are always accompanied by the definite article: il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie (my), il tuo, la tua etc. The article agrees with the noun owned, not the owner. Important exception: singular unmodified family members drop the article — 'mio padre' (not il mio padre), 'mia madre', 'mio fratello'. This exception does not apply with 'loro' (il loro padre) or with modified/plural family nouns.

examples.en: my father (singular family member — no article)
their father (loro always keeps the article)

title: Ogni — every
explanation: 'Ogni' (every) is invariable and always takes a singular noun, regardless of meaning. It does not change form for gender.
